name: Spreadsheet Grid
summary: Arrow keys move, Enter commits and drops a row, Tab commits and moves right, typing replaces, Escape reverts. The cell contract everyone knows from Excel and almost nobody ships on the web.

attempts.prompt: Build an editable table where you can click a cell and change its value.
attempts.problem: Every cell became an input, so the grid rendered forty form controls, Tab walked through all of them one by one, and arrow keys moved the caret inside a field rather than moving between cells. Typing appended to the existing value instead of replacing it. There was no distinction between a selected cell and a cell being edited, which is the distinction the entire interaction model rests on.

attempts.prompt: Use a roving tabindex and only turn a cell into an input when editing.
attempts.problem: Navigation worked, but Enter and Tab behaved identically — both just moved — when a spreadsheet gives them different jobs: Enter commits and drops a row, Tab commits and moves right. Escape was unhandled, so a mistaken edit could not be abandoned. Committing an edit left focus in limbo because the input was removed before focus was moved back to the cell.

finalPrompt:
Build an editable data grid in plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, no dependencies, using a real table element.

This component is defined by its keyboard contract, not by its appearance. Implement it exactly:

Arrow keys move the selection one cell. Home and End move to the first and last cell of the row. Tab commits any edit and moves right; Shift+Tab commits and moves left. Enter on a selected cell begins editing; Enter while editing commits and moves down one row. F2 begins editing without clearing. Escape while editing reverts that cell to the value it held when editing began and stays put. Delete or Backspace on a selected cell clears it without entering edit mode. Any printable character begins editing with that character, replacing the previous contents.

The distinction between selected and editing is the model, so make it structural: exactly one cell carries tabindex="0" and all others carry -1, editing is a data attribute on the cell, and the two states are styled differently — selection as an inset ring the eye can find across a dense grid, editing as a caret in a plain field.

Do not render inputs. Use contenteditable="plaintext-only" on the cell itself, switched on when editing begins and off when it ends, so the table contains forty cells rather than forty form controls and Tab does not walk through them.

On commit, place the caret correctly: select all contents when editing starts from F2 or Enter, collapse to the end when it starts from a typed character.

Mark a cell whose value changed with a data attribute and show it as a small dot, so uncommitted work is visible.

Give the table a visually hidden caption stating the keyboard contract, real column headers with scope="col", and row headers with scope="row".

Colour comes only from CSS custom properties: var(--bg), var(--raised), var(--border), var(--text), var(--text-dim), var(--accent), with color-mix for the selection tint. No literal hex, rgb or hsl values.
why:
Almost everything that makes this component right is invisible in a screenshot, which is why both earlier attempts looked finished and felt wrong.

The key move was writing the keyboard contract as a specification rather than asking for keyboard support. Eleven keys, each with a stated job, and crucially the two that people conflate: Enter commits and drops, Tab commits and moves right. A model asked for "keyboard navigation" will make those the same because both plausibly mean next.

The second lesson is that forbidding an implementation can be more useful than describing one. Saying do not render inputs, use contenteditable on the cell, removed a whole class of problems at once — the tab-order pollution, the focus-restoration bug, the forty-controls performance issue — none of which I would have had to enumerate.

When a component is a contract people already know, transcribe the contract. Do not describe the feeling of it.
